The segmental stilbene-like ligand E- DiL1 displays only an irreversible E → Z photoisomerization under UV-light irradiation due to the overlapping of its absorption spectrum with that of its isomer Z-DiL1, which is further hampered by competing prejudicial intra/intermolecular photoreactions. These limitations can be overcome by exploiting the conformational and electronic changes induced upon connecting E-DiL1 to [Y(hfac)3] rare earth cargoes. In the target {E-DiL1[Y(hfac)3]2} adduct, the connection of the electron-withdrawing Y(III) guest extends the aromatic delocalization and shifts the absorption band to the red. This restores a clean E-to-Z isomer switching of the bridging stilbene-like unit upon visible light irradiation at 420 nm or by simple exposition to room light. The steric hindrance induced by the [Y(hfac)3] containers also prevents detrimental competing photoreactions. The electronic decoupling of the two terimine units in the photoisomerized {Z-DiL1[Y(hfac)3]2} adduct gives rise to a blue shift of the ligand-centered 1π* ← 1π transition and the operation of reverse Z-to-E photoisomerization upon selective near-UV excitation at 380 nm. The guest-induced enlargement of the amplitude of specific excitation wavelengths for inducing E-to-Z and Z-to-E photoisomerizations paves the way for selective signaling in biocompatible environments.

item.title: ACS Nano: Reactive Oxygen Species-Responsive Diselenide-Bridged Silica Nanoparticles Reprogram Ferroptosis for Inflammatory Bowel Disease Therapy
item.description:
Tongfei Shi, Ying Zhou, Jiaqi Xu, Yifan Zhou, Xuenian Chen, Xin Zhao, Xiaochun Xie, Ziping Wu, et al.
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is driven by persistent epithelial injury and unresolved immune activation, yet effective therapies remain limited by an incomplete understanding of its spatiotemporal pathological mechanisms. Here, single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals a previously unrecognized ferroptotic landscape in intestinal mucosa, characterized by rapid depletion of ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) in epithelial cells followed by delayed exhaustion of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) in macrophages. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we engineered a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive nanoselenium to deliver ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) by a diselenide-bridged silica carrier to achieve spatiotemporal ferroptosis regulation. In response to pathological ROS, our nanoplatform rapidly releases Fer-1 to alleviate epithelial injury and maintain barrier integrity, followed by sustained selenium release to reactivate macrophage GPX4, thereby resolving the inflammatory responses. This sequential ferroptosis intervention effectively disrupts the pathogenic interplay between epithelial damage and inflammatory amplification, leading to a robust recovery of intestinal architecture and immune homeostasis with excellent biocompatibility. Collectively, our work identifies ferroptosis as a mechanistic link between epithelial dysfunction and immune dysregulation and establishes a mechanism-guided nanomedicine paradigm for spatiotemporal regulation of inflammatory bowel disease.

item.title: JACS: A Cryptic Cytochrome P450 Radical Cyclase Catalyzes Naphthalene-Ring Closure in Rifamycin Biosynthesis
item.description:
Feng Ye, Lingfei Hu, Meng Niu, Yanrong Shi, Zhongyue Li, Gang Lu, Yuemao Shen
The enzymatic assembly of the 8-hydroxynaphthalene chromophore in rifamycins presents a classic biosynthetic paradox: the off-PKS precursor, prorifamycin A (1a), readily suffers nonenzymatic deoxygenative collapse in solution into the aberrant product 8-deoxynaphthoquinones. Here, using in cellulo genetic manipulation, stepwise pathway reconstitution, in vitro enzymatic assays, molecular docking, and DFT calculations, we identified Rif-Orf0 to be a cytochrome P450 radical cyclase. Rif-Orf0 converted 1a to the 8-hydroxy-7,8-dihydronaphthalenoid intermediate prorifamycin B (1b) through a low-barrier biradical cyclization, and the RifS/RifT dehydrogenase pair rapidly captured and oxidatively aromatized 1b to 34a-deoxyrifamycin W (2). This Rif-Orf0 and RifS/RifT enzymatic cascade outcompeted the spontaneous deoxygenative shunting that afforded 8-deoxynaphthalene-type rifamycins, thereby enforcing the production of 8-hydroxynaphthalenoid rifamycins. This study expanded the catalytic repertoire of cytochrome P450 enzymes and resolved a long-standing question in rifamycin biosynthesis by characterizing how tailoring enzymes canalized reactive intermediates from spontaneous reactions toward defined natural product architectures.

item.title: JACS: Water-Soluble Pd12 Multicomponent Cage Enables Selective Separation of 1,4-Dibromonaphthalene from 1,5-Dibromonaphthalene and Regioselective Bromination of Naphthalene
item.description:
Pooja Singh, Ranit Banerjee, Jack K. Clegg, Partha Sarathi Mukherjee
The synthesis of intricate supramolecular architectures is driven by the desire to translate structural complexity into functional specificity. Herein, we report the formation of an unusual M12L4L′4 cage (MCC) with double-walled knotted architecture via multicomponent self-assembly of a tripyridyl ligand (L), a tricarboxylate ligand (L′), and a cis-Pd(II) acceptor (M). The structure of the MCC resembles a truncated tetrahedron with two overlaid walls enclosing a distorted cavity. The cavity selectively encapsulates polyaromatic hydrocarbons with two fused rings like naphthalene (G1) and its derivatives [1,4-dibromonaphthalene (G5) and 1,5-dibromonaphthalene (G6)], while it is repellent to larger guests in aqueous media. Interestingly, it shows high selectivity for 1,4-dibromonaphthalene (G5), which enabled the purification of 1,4-dibromonaphthalene and 1,5-dibromonaphthalene (G6) from their mixture in aqueous media. Furthermore, selective bromination of naphthalene to 1,4-dibromonaphthalene could be achieved within the hydrophobic cavity of MCC in aqueous media under ambient reaction conditions driven by the high specificity of the cavity for G5, while the same bromination in the absence of the cage yields a mixture of dibromo and monobromo derivatives. Thus, the newly designed cage (MCC) could be utilized for developing an efficient strategy for the regioselective bromination of naphthalene, overcoming the challenges associated with separating the product mixture generated in conventional bromination. Moreover, the cage enables efficient separation of the dibromo isomers of naphthalene formed in conventional synthesis.

item.title: JACS: Cascade Synthesis of Alternating Thiolactone–Episulfide Copolymers via Multi-Site Single-Unit Monomer Insertion
item.description:
Yu Xiong, Shun-Ran Peng, Zong-Bin Lu, Zhe Wang, Guang Chen, Wei-Qiang Huang, Xuan Nie, Chun-Yan Hong, et al.
Alternating copolymers are fundamental sequence-controlled polymers, but their synthesis from two independently polymerizable monomers remains challenging because conventional methods rely on selective cross-propagation, limiting monomer combinations and structural diversity. Here, we report a two-step cascade strategy that decouples sequence control from direct alternating copolymerization. We target thiolactones and episulfides, important sulfur-containing heterocycles accessible from biobased or low-cost feedstocks. However, competing homopolymerization pathways in many thiolactone–episulfide combinations complicate their direct alternating copolymerization. In our approach, controlled thiolactone ring-opening polymerization affords well-defined polythioesters, followed by selective episulfide single-unit monomer insertion (SUMI) at every thioester linkage to yield perfectly alternating poly(thioether-thioester)s. This transformation is enabled by S-aryl thioester-mediated SUMI, wherein facile aryl thiolate departure promotes efficient single insertion while suppressing further propagation. Using inexpensive quaternary onium salts without stringent stoichiometric or reaction-time control, the method furnishes 23 new sulfur-rich alternating copolymers with molecular weights up to 157.1 kDa, tensile strengths up to 75.2 MPa, and Young’s moduli up to 2.24 GPa. This cascade route expands the accessible sequence-defined polymer space and creates new opportunities to tailor their properties and functions.

item.title: JACS: Photoaffinity Capture of Unit-Resolved Ubiquitin–Decoder Contacts Underlying Topology-Selective Recognition of Heterotypic Chains
item.description:
Takafumi Furuhata, Taiki Uno, Ryota Shinohara, Takuya Tomita, Usano Toyoda, Tokiha Masuda-Ozawa, Yasushi Saeki, Akimitsu Okamoto
Heterotypic K63/K48 polyubiquitin chains encode diverse cellular outcomes, ranging from proteasomal degradation to nonproteolytic signaling. Although chain topology is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of these functions, how architectures composed of the same linkage types are decoded into distinct outputs remains poorly understood. This gap has persisted because molecular technologies capable of both chemically capturing topology-selective decoders and defining the unit-resolved contacts underlying selective recognition remain undeveloped. Here we report diazirine-functionalized K63/K48 triubiquitin probes that resolve the unit-specific ubiquitin–decoder contacts essential for topology-selective decoding of the K63/K48 chains with distinct branch architectures. Site-specific installation of a single diazirine moiety into defined ubiquitin units enabled systematic interrogation of the contributions of individual ubiquitin units to topology-selective recognition by quantifying their engagement with decoders through photo-cross-linking efficiency. Specifically, the mixed K63/K48 tribuiquitin (Ub3) probes with diazirine on the K63-linked segment captured a previously unrecognized preference of OTUB1 and RAD23B for mixed K63/K48 chains through more efficient photo-cross-linking than the corresponding branched K63/K48 Ub3 probes. In addition, liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) analysis of the cross-linked products identified auxiliary contacts of the K63-linked segment in mixed K63/K48 Ub3 as the molecular basis for the topology-selective recognition by OTUB1 and RAD23B. Thus, these chemically defined photoaffinity K63/K48 chains provide a versatile platform for dissecting the molecular logic by which heterotypic ubiquitin-chain topologies are decoded into distinct intracellular outputs.

item.title: JACS: Symmetry-Breaking Charge Localization Controls Radiationless Decay in a Multibranched Charge-Transfer State
item.description:
Joy Jerome, Bishnu Pokhrel, Nishant Dhiman, Seema Rani, Shahnawaz R. Rather
Symmetry breaking in multibranched charge-transfer (CT) excited states is generally viewed as a mechanism for excited-state localization, yet how such localization controls the subsequent fate of the excitation remains poorly understood. Here, we show that environmental stabilization of a symmetry-broken CT state can fundamentally reshape radiationless decay in a bent donor–acceptor–donor chromophore. Increasing solvent stabilization drives rapid reorganization toward a lower-energy CT configuration, collapsing the singlet lifetime from 1.98 ns in toluene to 9.2 ps in acetonitrile while increasing the effective nonradiative rate (knr) from 2.14 × 108 to >1.11 × 1011 s–1. Femtosecond transient absorption establishes that formation of the stabilized CT configuration precedes terminal population loss, while triplet accumulation observed in nonpolar media disappears as singlet depletion becomes ultrafast. Controlled toluene–acetonitrile mixtures further reveal that the nonradiative rate does not obey a single invariant energy-gap dependence: distinct energy-gap-law regimes emerge as the CT state is progressively stabilized, followed by a strongly reorganized regime in which knr continues to accelerate despite little additional change in the energy gap. Independently, the changing relationship between emission spectral variance and Stokes shift shows that the nuclear reorganization of the relaxed CT ensemble also changes with stabilization. Together, these results support a solvent-dependent symmetry-breaking landscape in which progressive charge localization reshapes both the excited-state energy and the nuclear coordinates governing access to the ground state. Symmetry breaking therefore acts not simply as an electronic localization process, but as an environmental kinetic switch, converting a long-lived, emissive and triplet-forming CT state into a rapidly quenched excited state.

item.title: ACS Nano: Marine-Inspired Small Extracellular Vesicle-Loaded Wet-Adhesive Hydrogel with Sr2+ Release Enables Immunomodulatory Cartilage Regeneration via Wnt/β-Catenin Inhibition
item.description:
Houxi Li, Shuhang Dong, Luqi Yang, Guangyu Li, Haiyan Li, Zehua Wang, Shiyuan Xue, Jiakui Ren, et al.
Effective cartilage repair remains challenging because hydrogel-based strategies must coordinate structural support, sustained delivery of regenerative cues, immune microenvironment remodeling, and pathway-directed chondrogenic regulation. Here, we report a marine-inspired multifunctional hydrogel, termed GMPSE, constructed by incorporating polydopamine nanoparticles (PDA-NPs), strontium ions (Sr2+), and bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicle (BMSC-sEV)-enriched preparation into a fish-scale-derived methacrylated gelatin (GelMA). GelMA provides an injectable and photo-cross-linkable matrix for conformal defect filling, PDA-NPs contribute to the adhesive and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging properties of the formulation, Sr2+ provides sustained ionic stimulation, and BMSC-sEVs serve as cell-free paracrine regulators. GMPSE exhibited a homogeneous porous architecture, favorable injectability, elastic-dominated viscoelastic behavior, lap-shear adhesion on glass substrates, and sustained release of both Sr2+ and BMSC-sEVs. Ex vivo lap-shear testing of porcine cartilage–hydrogel–glass assemblies after 10 min of water immersion yielded a nominal apparent strength of approximately 62.4 kPa for GMPSE. In vitro, GMPSE supported chondrocyte viability, spreading, migration, and three-dimensional survival, reduced intracellular ROS levels, attenuated inflammatory macrophage activation and promoted a repair-associated marker profile, and enhanced BMSC chondrogenic differentiation, as evidenced by increased SOX9, collagen type II, and aggrecan expression. Transcriptomic profiling and pathway-reactivation experiments supported a contribution of canonical Wnt/β-catenin suppression to GMPSE-enhanced chondrogenesis. In an acute osteochondral model, GMPSE promoted defect filling and cartilage-like repair tissue formation, supported subchondral bone repair, and increased CD206-associated staining in the repair region at 12 weeks. Overall, this study presents a marine-derived, wet-adhesive, immunomodulatory, and cell-free bioactive hydrogel platform for minimally invasive cartilage regeneration.

item.title: Nano Letters: Proximity-Triggered DNA Self-Assembly for Selective Regulation of Membrane Receptors on Living Cells
item.description:
Ajiao Sun, Xuran Dai, Jiaxin Jia, Xueqi Zhao, Yuchuan Liu, Daqian Song, Ying Sun
Membrane receptors activate downstream signaling through oligomerization to regulate cellular behaviors, yet selectively modulating membrane receptor signaling in cancer cells remains challenging. Here, we report a proximity-triggered DNA self-assembly (PTDSA) strategy for cancer-cell-selective receptor regulation. PTDSA uses aptamers targeting the cancer-cell biomarker EpCAM and receptor c-Met as proximity triggers. Only when EpCAM and c-Met are simultaneously bound and spatially proximal does toehold-mediated strand displacement initiate catalytic hairpin assembly, generating a proximity-triggered hybrid intermediate. Through programmable DNA sequences, this intermediate recruits probe-bound lysosomal shuttling receptors (IGFIIR) to form functional PTDSA complexes. These complexes hijack lysosomal trafficking pathways to deliver c-Met for degradation, thereby suppressing downstream oncogenic signaling. In HeLa cells, PTDSA achieved 35% c-Met degradation and inhibited cell migration by 33%. This work establishes PTDSA as a DNA-programmable platform for cancer-cell-selective membrane receptor degradation and modulation, offering a strategy to overcome the nonspecificity of conventional receptor-targeting approaches.

item.title: ACS Nano: Bioorthogonal Engineering of Tumors with Bacterial Antigens Leverages Innate Immunity for Enhanced Adoptive T Cell Therapy
item.description:
Wen-Fang Song, Rui-Lin Li, Ping Ji, Wen Li, Wei-Qin Yao, Jun Feng, Xuan Zeng, Xian-Zheng Zhang
Substantial efforts in adoptive T-cell therapy have centered on boosting T-cell activity against tumors. However, a crucial yet overlooked factor is that the onset and maintenance of T-cell responses are highly dependent on innate immunity. Here, we developed a strategy of engineering tumors with bacterial antigens via click chemistry to cross-regulate innate-adaptive immunity, thereby enhancing the efficacy of adoptive T-cell therapy in solid tumors. The targeted delivery of bacterial antigens is mediated by azido sugar liposomes (TALP) for introducing azide groups on tumors and dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated bacterial membranes (DBCO-BM) to endow tumor cells with the innate immunogenicity of bacteria. Our study reveals that tumors with exposed bacterial antigens trigger innate immune responses for direct tumor killing and drive T-cell tumor infiltration to launch adaptive immunity. The antitumor functions of adoptive T cells are significantly augmented with the cross-activation of innate-adaptive immunity. This study highlights the potential of innate immunity in addressing the suboptimal response of adoptive T cells in solid tumors.

item.title: ACS Nano: AI-Driven Cross-Scale Simulation of Lithium Batteries
item.description:
Qiliang Zhang, Juntao Zhao, Hanming Li, Peiyu Chen, Genming Lai, Zekai Liu, Jianwei Li, Ruiqi Zhang, et al.
The evolution of lithium battery performance involves complex coupled processes across multiple scales, ranging from electronic and atomic scales to mesoscopic structures and battery systems. Traditional simulation approaches face significant challenges in accurately predicting realistic battery electrochemical responses because of scale-bridging limitations, high computational costs, and insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms. In recent years, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have provided opportunities for cross-scale simulations by enabling knowledge transfer and intelligent prediction through learning physical representations from data. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The review first discusses AI-enabled simulation approaches spanning the micro- to mesoscale, including machine learning potentials (MLPs), AI-driven kinetic Monte Carlo (AI-kMC), AI-driven phase-field modeling (AI-PFM), and AI-driven coarse-grained molecular dynamics (AI-CGMD). It then summarizes meso- to macroscale methodologies, including surrogate models, reduced-order modeling, and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Furthermore, AI applications in multiscale feature fusion, inverse materials design, and battery design automation (BDA) are discussed together with computational paradigms toward digital twins and intelligent battery research and development. Despite substantial advances, several critical challenges, including limited model generalization and insufficient uncertainty quantification, remain. Integrating foundation models, generative AI, and multiscale physical modeling could enable more accurate and computationally efficient battery simulation frameworks. These advances may accelerate the discovery, optimization, and deployment of next-generation energy-storage technologies.

item.title: JACS: Aryl Palladium Acetates as Highly Active Species in Intermolecular Heck Reactions of Hindered Olefins
item.description:
Jingyao Hu, Bo Xiao, Xiuhua Wang, Jianrong Steve Zhou
Despite decades of development since the early 1970s, the intermolecular Heck reaction of hindered tri- and tetrasubstituted olefins with aryl halides has remained a challenge. Traditional approaches relied on rate-acceleration by directing groups or high reactivity of cationic arylpalladium species generated from triflates and diazonium salts. Herein, we report the first general and efficient Heck coupling between trisubstituted alkenes (and selected tetrasubstituted olefins) with aryl iodides and bromides. Our protocol employs simple PdCl2 or Pd(OAc)2 as precatalyst and needs no directing groups. It features an exceptionally broad substrate scope, accommodating diverse (hetero)aryl halides and both acyclic and cyclic olefins, and the reaction proceeds efficiently on a gram scale with remarkably low palladium loadings. The practical value of this method is highlighted by its application in concise synthesis of several pharmaceutically relevant motifs. Mechanistically, HRMS and DFT calculations revealed that phosphine-free complexes of arylpalladium acetates─either monomer [(Ar)Pd(OAc)] or its paddlewheel dimer with bridging acetates─serve as the key active species. These species exhibit minimal steric hindrance, a high partial positive charge, and high electrophilicity at the palladium center, synergistically facilitating the binding and rapid insertion of hindered alkenes.

item.title: JACS: Spatiotemporally Decoupled Cascade Photocatalysis on Dual S-Scheme Heterostructure with Interfacial Polarization Fields and Proton Shuttle Channels
item.description:
Yi-Wen Han, Run-Yu Liu, Lei Ye, Yu-Xin Zhang, Yao Fu
Transient surface reaction dynamics govern artificial-photosynthesis-enabled multistep tandem biomass oxidation but are hindered by spatially intermingled reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and temporally entangled elementary-step sequences. A spatial-engineering strategy for fabricating ZnS/Sv-chalcogenide/MoSe2 (Sv = sulfur vacancies, chalcogenide = ZnIn2S4, Zn0.5Cd0.5S, CdIn2S4) dual S-scheme heterostructure, with chalcogenide as the shared mediator between the ZnS/chalcogenide and chalcogenide/MoSe2 S-junctions, is developed by anchoring MoSe2 nanoparticles onto chalcogenide nanosheets epitaxially grown from ZnS hollow dodecahedral cages. These ternary-component nanoreactors integrate dual interfacial features, the interfacial localized polarization field and the interfacial proton shuttle channel, to orchestrate dynamic intelligent catalysis. Specifically, the interfacial localized polarization field drives spatially decoupled ROS generation (•OH, •O2–, •OOH) via the asymmetric charge distributions, enabling zone-specific ROS to undertake differentiated oxidation tasks. Interfacial proton shuttle channel drives temporally decoupled elementary-step sequences via the interfacial dynamic hydrogen-bonding networks, thereby liberating pH-dependent proton transfer through directed radical protonation (•O2– → •OOH). This synergy provides a proof of concept for neutral 5-hydroxymethylfurfural-to-2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (HMF-to-FDCA) conversion and demonstrates a fundamental research-to-practical-application capability. This work proposes a generalizable catalyst design paradigm integrating interfacial localized polarization fields and interfacial proton shuttle channels, offering innovative insights for guiding spatiotemporally decoupled multistep cascade catalysis.

item.title: ACS Nano: Atomic Bridges Directionally Assemble Nanoclusters into Conductive Nanowires for Enhanced CO2 Electroreduction
item.description:
Ke Zhu, Chengqi Li, Yang Wang, Yuanxin Du, Hongting Sheng, Manzhou Zhu
One-dimensional (1D) nanowires, owing to their directional charge transport properties, represent an excellent catalytic platform for overcoming electron and proton transport bottlenecks in electrocatalysis. In this work, we directionally assemble discrete Cu6 nanoclusters into Cu6 nanowires (Cu6-NWs) using an atomically designed “atomic bridge”, achieving long-range order at the atomic scale. The resulting Cu6-NWs exhibit an electrical conductivity of 8.2 × 10–4 S·cm–1, which is 8 orders of magnitude higher than that of discrete Cu6 nanoclusters, highlighting the superiority of the wire-like ordered structure in charge transport. In the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), Cu6-NWs achieve a Faraday efficiency (FE) of 64.8% for hydrocarbon products (CH4 and C2H4) at −1.1 V, reversing the hydrogen evolution-dominated catalytic behavior observed for isolated Cu6 nanoclusters. Mechanistic studies reveal that the linear configuration of Cu6-NWs strengthens the coupling between electron and proton transport. Moreover, it modulates the d-band center via active-site migration, thereby tuning the activity and selectivity of CO2RR. The atomic-bridge-directed assembly strategy offers a perspective for designing high-performance catalysts.

item.title: JACS: Phototunable Solid–Liquid Interfacial Energy via Ion–Electron Coupling
item.description:
Seongmin Park, Hyunbae Cheon, Dongho Shin, Daeho Kim, Wooseop Lee, Huding Jin, Junwoo Park
The solid–liquid interfacial energy governs wetting, adhesion, and friction, yet is commonly regarded as a static property defined by surface chemistry and liquid composition. Here we show that light can reversibly modulate the interfacial energy at chemically invariant semiconductor–electrolyte interfaces by tuning the electrostatic coupling between electronic carriers in the solid and ions in the liquid. Using dark dynamic tensiometry, we directly quantify photoinduced changes in advancing and receding contact angles, revealing pronounced and reversible wettability modulation that is absent on insulating or metallic substrates. Systematic control experiments indicate that, in simple salt electrolytes, the response arises primarily from electrostatic coupling between photomodulated carriers and mobile ions in the electric double layer, rather than from detectable photochemical surface modification or changes in bulk liquid properties. In situ atomic force microscopy and ionovoltaic measurements provide microscopic and quantitative evidence that light attenuates or enhances electrostatic double-layer forces and ion–electron coupling, and reveal a sign reversal in the photoresponse between PFOTS-modified and bare Si interfaces. The opposing responses of PFOTS-modified and bare interfaces persist on p-type Si, showing that the effect is not confined to n-type substrates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phototunable coupling extends to reversible control of kinetic friction, enabling active modulation of droplet sliding dynamics. These results also identify imaging light as a potential source of bias in contact-angle measurements at photoactive semiconductor–electrolyte interfaces. These findings establish ion–electron coupling as a tunable thermodynamic lever linking semiconductor physics to macroscopic interfacial energy, opening opportunities for optically controlled wetting, friction, and interfacial transport.

item.title: ACS Nano: Nanozyme-Fortified Probiotics with Antioxidant and Anti-Infection Properties for Synergistic Living Therapeutics of Infected Diabetic Wounds
item.description:
Yan-Ting Han, Jia-Cheng Lv, Ting-Ting Hu, Zi-Han Chen, Na Li, Xi Liao, Jia-Zhuang Xu, Zhi-Guo Wang, et al.
Living probiotics are receiving considerable attention in serving as biosafe and superb antibacterial agents for infected wound healing. However, the inadequate reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging capacity compromises the therapeutic effect of probiotics for infected diabetic wounds with high oxidative stress. Herein, we develop a nanozyme-fortified probiotic (NFP) orchestrating an excellent antioxidative activity and broad-spectrum antibacterial properties for synergistic living therapeutics of infected diabetic wounds. The Cu-doped zinc metal–organic framework (CDN) is synthesized to provide a bimetallic biomimetic Cu/Zn site and is uniformly anchored on the surface of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG). The resultant NFP exhibits four types of enzyme-like catalytic activities for ROS scavenging and demonstrates an excellent antioxidant capability. The superior intracellular antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of NFP are also perceived, ascribed to the regulation of cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, arachidonic acid metabolism, and signaling by interleukins in the cell. The secretion promotion of antimicrobial short-chain fatty acids is triggered by CDN regulation for the physiological activities of LGG, eliciting the well-balanced antibacterial activity of NFP. As demonstrated by the rat model of infected diabetic wounds, application of NFP significantly eradicates bacterial infection, alleviates inflammation by ROS elimination, and directs polarization to M2 macrophages, thereby accelerating wound closure. This work provides a promising living material-based tactic consisting of microbial therapy and catalytic nanomaterials for treating infected diabetic wounds.

item.title: JACS: Discerning between Excimer and Singlet Fission Sites Using Modulated Magnetic Field Photoluminescence
item.description:
Jessica R. Walton, Miles I. Collins, Rachel C. Kilbride, Daniel T. W. Toolan, Lars van Turnhout, Olivier Paré-Labrosse, Dane R. McCamey, Christiane Timmel, et al.
Magnetic field effects play a key role in the characterization of organic electronic materials. In particular, the microscopic processes underlying singlet fission and triplet–triplet annihilation have been clarified in recent years through the observation and subsequent theoretical explanation of magnetic field effects in these processes. Here, we study magnetic field effects on the luminescence of 5,12-bis((triisopropylsilyl)ethynyl)tetracene, a well-studied material in which both singlet fission and triplet–triplet annihilation occur. By performing highly sensitive modulated-field magneto-photoluminescence experiments we observe magnetic field effect lineshapes with rich detail, allowing a precise characterization of triplet exciton dynamics. By additionally filtering these magnetic field effects by luminescence wavelength, we can identify the excimer state by its unique magnetic field signature. Finally, we show that a theoretical explanation of these field effects requires a model that explicitly accounts for quantum coherences, which highlights the importance of detailed spin dynamics modeling in understanding magnetic field effects, even at room temperature.

item.title: JACS: Cathode Surface Reconfiguration via Solvent Chemistry for Durable All-Solid-State Lithium Batteries
item.description:
Zi-Yi Zhou, Ru-Meng Wu, Man-Yi Xie, Lu Gan, Yao Zhao, Ji-Lei Shi, Yue Gong, Yu-Guo Guo, et al.
Electrode surfaces and interfaces critically dominate the performance of all-solid-state lithium batteries. However, established additive-oriented strategies physically isolate the cathode from the electrolyte without improving the restricted Li+ transport pathways of the cathode surface. Here, we propose a solvation-mediated chemical etching mechanism governing cathode surface reconfiguration, driven by competition between solvent coordination and lattice stabilization. The solvent coordination, coupled with electron and proton transfer, weakens transition-metal–oxygen covalency and destabilizes lattice-bound surface species, shifting the interfacial energy landscape toward solvation-favored states. This triggers selective transition-metal dissolution and oxygen modulation, ultimately reorganizing confined surface regions into continuous Li+ transport networks. Using micron-sized single-crystalline Li- and Mn-rich cathodes as a model, we demonstrate the formation of a Mn- and O-deficient interfacial layer equipped with a three-dimensional Li+ diffusion network. This functional layer accelerates Li+ diffusion and anionic redox kinetics while suppressing transition metal migration and oxygen release. Consequently, charge-transfer resistance drops drastically (from 585 to 67 Ω) and Li+ diffusion increases 90-fold at 4.8 V, enabling 80.3% capacity retention after 2800 cycles at 2C. This solvent-driven reconfiguration provides a scalable framework for stabilizing diverse cathodes in next-generation advanced batteries.

item.title: JACS: Concerted Ligand-to-Metal Charge Transfer Absorption and Localized Photoluminescence in an Fe(III) Photosensitizer
item.description:
Matthew Goodwin, Jinkai Cheng, Felix Glaser, Ludovic Troian-Gautier, Gerald J. Meyer
There is tremendous interest in the electronic structure of [FeIII(phtmeimb)2]+, the first iron complex to show room temperature photoluminescence (PL) with an excited-state lifetime sufficient for dynamic quenching in fluid solution. Two types of excited states are generated by light absorption, termed the Franck–Condon (FC) state and the thermally equilibrated excited state (THEXI) that is photoluminescent. Herein we report solvatochromic and electroabsorption studies to probe the electronic structure of these two states. The doublet ligand-to-metal-charge-transfer absorption was found to be mostly solvent independent while a notable solvatochromism in the PL spectra indicated the presence of an excited-state dipole in polar solvents (μ⃗ = 16 ± 10 D), best formulated as [FeII(phtmeimb•+)(phtmeimb)]+*. However, standard and higher-order electroabsorption spectra revealed concerted and equal charge transfer from the two tridentate ligands to the metal, giving rise to a significant polarizability change (Δα) without the generation of a dipole moment (Δμ⃗ = 0) best formulated as [FeII(phtmeimb+1/2)2]+*. The strong interligand coupling necessary for such concerted charge transfer is proposed to be mediated by a t2g orbital of the Fe(III) center. Taken together, these findings provide new insights into this famed photoluminescent open-shell iron complex relevant to the design of improved iron photosensitizers.

item.title: JACS: Taming Metal–Electrolyte Interface via Two-Dimensional Organic Metal Chalcogenide Colloids for Anode-Free Sodium Metal Batteries
item.description:
Chaozhi Wang, Xiaoqing Yu, Ruixuan Qin, Jingqin Cui, Shuchang Liu, Cuimiao Wang, Chen Yang, Qiulong Wei, et al.
Anode-free metal batteries are promising candidates for next-generation energy storage technologies, yet their application is severely limited by dendrite growth and rapid capacity decay induced by an unstable metal–electrolyte interface. Herein, we propose a “colloid electrolyte” strategy employing coordination polymer nanosheets as electrolyte additives for constructing anode-free sodium metal batteries (AFSMBs). Unlike conventional molecular additives or inert particle suspensions, these colloidal nanosheets provide spatially organized and continuously available interfacial reaction domains, thereby spatially regulating electrolyte component distribution and interfacial reactions. These nanosheets, composed of AgS layers uniformly decorated with fluorinated groups, undergo in situ decomposition at the metal–electrolyte interface. This process generates gradient distributions of Ag nanoparticles and NaF/Na2S species, which guide the spontaneous formation of a functionally graded solid electrolyte interphase (SEI). This hierarchical SEI enables dendrite-free Na deposition and imparts sustained interfacial protection during cycling. Consequently, high-cathode-loading AFSMBs achieve an ultralong lifespan (>1600 cycles), representing a 10-fold improvement over counterpart cells without the colloidal additive. Notably, 0.5-Ah-level anode-free pouch cells exhibit stable cycling for 500 cycles at 2 C. This work establishes coordination polymer colloids as a new class of electrolyte additives for advanced alkali metal batteries.

item.title: ACS Nano: Weakly Exothermic Intermetallic NiBi Anode Enables Ultrafine Reconstruction for High-Rate Sodium-Ion Storage
item.description:
Guoping Liu, Zhiming Jia, Zhipeng Sun, Wentong Chen, Chaofeng Zhang
Bismuth (Bi) anodes are attractive for sodium-ion batteries due to their high capacity and inherent self-reconstruction into bicontinuous porous structures during cycling. However, rapid surface diffusion of Bi atoms during desodiation causes severe ligament coarsening, which compromises both rate capability and cycling reversibility. Here, we introduce a weakly exothermic intermetallic NiBi anode with small formation energy to address this challenge. The close electronegativity between Ni and Bi results in a small formation energy and metallic conductivity, which favor efficient electron transport and facilitate the breaking and recombination of Ni–Bi bonds during cycling. Meanwhile, the interatomic bonding between Ni and Bi effectively suppresses Bi diffusion and inhibits ligament coarsening during desodiation, enabling NiBi to evolve into an ultrafine bicontinuous porous network with an average ligament size of only 65.3 nm, about three times finer than that of pure Bi. As a result, the NiBi anode achieves a high initial Coulombic efficiency of 91.09%, a reversible capacity of 304.2 mAh g–1, excellent rate capability, and an outstanding lifespan of 20,000 cycles with 93.1% capacity retention. This work demonstrates that weakly exothermic intermetallic design with small formation energy offers a promising route to regulate reconstruction and suppress coarsening for durable sodium storage.

item.title: JACS: Extraframework Cations Promoted Ultratrace Acetylene Capture by Coordinatively Unsaturated Nickel Sites in FAU Zeolites
item.description:
Jian Wang, Jiarui Fan, Bin Yue, Bin Qin, Shanshan Liu, Yuchao Chai, Guangjun Wu, Pascal Manuel, et al.
Removal of ultratrace alkynes to produce polymer- and electronic-grade olefins is an important but extremely challenging task. Here, we report a dual-cation strategy in FAU-type zeolites that enables the unprecedented capture of acetylene at concentrations of parts per million (ppm). The optimized Ni–Ba–Y adsorbent delivers high dynamic uptakes of 0.37–0.82 mmol·g–1 at acetylene concentrations of 500–10,000 ppm, with acetylene/ethylene selectivity exceeding 100 under industrial relevant conditions. Neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and theoretical calculations reveal that Ba2+ at Site I modulate the coordinatively unsaturated Ni2+ centers at Site II, enhancing π-back-donation to adsorbed acetylene. Process simulations demonstrate that adsorptive separation using Ni–Ba–Y achieves over 200-fold higher space-time productivity (STP) of ethylene and reduces energy consumption by over 44% compared with conventional catalytic hydrogenation processes. This dual-cation strategy will promote the design of zeolite adsorbents for challenging industrial separations.

item.title: ACS Nano: Spatial-Mechanical-Chemical Synergy in Inorganic-Shelled Cavities Enables Stable Li–Mg Alloy Anodes
item.description:
Yunlong Jiang, Zixuan Chen, Kai Deng, Tingting Li, Yuhang Liang, Rongkun Zheng, Yuanhui Zheng
Lithium metal batteries promise ultrahigh energy density yet are plagued by catastrophic lithium dendrites and severe volume expansion. Conventionally, rational three-dimensional (3D) host architectures have been developed to mitigate dendrite proliferation and mechanical stress. However, the structural collapse of lithium-hosting frameworks under dynamic plating/stripping conditions remains a critical bottleneck. Herein, we overcome this limitation by designing a Li-Mg alloy framework integrated with LiNO3 (LMLN), which yields in situ-formed cavities encapsulated by inorganic shells of high ionic conductivity that kinetically guide inward lithium deposition and promote uniform nucleation via tailored interfacial chemistry. The resulting spatial-mechanical-chemical coupling, realized by a scalable roller-pressing process, delivers a triadic synergy of spatially confined deposition, mechanically robust architecture, and chemically functional interfaces. Consequently, LMLN-based lithium metal batteries paired with commercial lithium-sulfur electrolytes and LiFePO4 (LFP) cathodes achieve 95.6% capacity retention over 300 cycles. Notably, a 1 Ah pouch cell pairing an 80 μm LMLN anode with a 17.5 mg cm–2 LFP cathode achieves 85.6% retention over 400 cycles at 1 C alongside intrinsic thermal safety under nail penetration. This dual achievement of superior 1 C cycle life and thermal robustness in 1 Ah LFP-Li metal pouch cells underscores its potential for moderate-rate, low-voltage storage applications.

item.title: ACS Nano: Self-Assembled Naphthalocyanine Molecular Lattices as a Platform for Tunable Quantum Superlattices
item.description:
Adrian Munther Bahri, Zhibo Kang, Ziyan Zhu, Eric I. Altman, Yu He, Chunjing Jia
Compared to van der Waals moiré systems, molecular assembly offers an alternative platform for superlattice engineering via heterointegration. The electronic properties of the self-assembled square-lattice monolayer of metal-free naphthalocyanine (H2Nc), in particular its band dispersion and tunability by metal substrates, remain less explored. Using density functional theory, we compare the electronic structure of a free-standing H2Nc monolayer with that of H2Nc lattices assembled on noble metal substrates. In the free-standing film, we identify nearly flat, molecule-localized states and more dispersive bands, each compactly described by an anisotropic tight-binding Hamiltonian yielding band-resolved hopping anisotropies. We further show theoretically the wide tunability of intersite hopping and Coulomb interaction through the dielectric and screening environment. On Ag(100), orbital hybridization between molecular frontier states and the substrate drives finite spectral weight at the Fermi level and local interfacial polarization, enhancing the effective intermolecular hopping roughly thirty-fold and drastically reducing U/t. Experimentally, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy resolves substantial interfacial charge redistribution and an enhanced bandwidth of the highest occupied molecular orbital, with the substrate coupling stronger on Ag(100) than Au(111), consistent with theory. Although static calculations exhibit an intrinsic C2 hopping anisotropy set by the two central hydrogens, thermal averaging over tautomer configurations at 77 K restores an effectively C4-symmetric dispersion while preserving the bandwidth. These results clarify how metal substrates and gates convert H2Nc from isolated molecules into a tunable 2D lattice, and highlight molecular superlattices as a platform in which effective interaction parameters can be widely engineered.

item.title: JACS: Transition-Metal-Mediated Discharge Intermediates Set Anionic-Redox Potentials and Voltage Hysteresis in Li-Rich Cathodes
item.description:
Yibo Wang, Ji Li, Lisheng Qian, Lifu Shen, Zhongqin Dai, Yande Li, Pengfei Yu, Xiaosong Liu
Voltage hysteresis arising from anionic redox reactions remains a central bottleneck for lithium-rich cathodes. While ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) has been invoked to describe the charging pathway, its proposed reverse counterpart, metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT), remains experimentally unresolved during discharge. Here, using cation-disordered rock-salt Li2Ni0.33Ta0.66O3 (LNTO) as a model system, we combine electrochemical relaxation analysis with synchrotron-based spectroscopy to identify, for the first time, a metastable reduction intermediate characterized by Ni(2-δ)+/(O–O)n− during discharge, thereby providing direct experimental validation for the MLCT framework. The discovery of this metastable intermediate demonstrates that discharge proceeds through a two-step electrochemical–chemical pathway, wherein the spontaneous relaxation evolution of the metastable intermediate drives free-energy dissipation and voltage hysteresis. Guided by this picture, Ru substitution was introduced to modulate the cation–anion electronic structure, enabling Ru 4d–O 2p hybridization to generate persistent low-energy hole states that lower the energy of the metastable discharge intermediate and shift O–O dimer reduction to higher potentials. We further show that the discharge intermediate serves as the energetic link through which transition-metal electronic structure governs the effective anionic-redox potential. This work provides a discharge-side thermodynamic framework for understanding and mitigating voltage hysteresis in Li-rich anionic-redox cathodes.

item.title: JACS: Electrothermal Mapping: A Methodology for Decoupling Redox, Protonation, and Denaturation Dynamics of Cytochrome c
item.description:
Alonso Gamero-Quijano, Carmen C. Tormo-Román, Miquel Á Galmés-Ordinas, José A. Manzanares, Miguel Alcalde, Marcos Pita, Micheál D. Scanlon, Antonio L. De Lacey
Differential scanning calorimetry, fluorometry, circular dichroism, and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry are routinely used to study thermal and chemical denaturation of proteins. However, these powerful methods monitor protein unfolding in bulk aqueous solutions but overlook interfacial environments, such as lipid membranes and confined crevices, where electrostatic and hydrophobic forces reshape protein conformational landscapes and dictate their function. Herein, we introduce an electrothermal methodology that uniquely probes protein conformational changes in a potential-modulated biomimetic environment. Electrochemistry at the Interface between Two Immiscible Electrolyte Solutions (ITIES) captures nonredox fingerprints of cytochrome c under heat stress, offering a unique perspective on protein behavior without relying on electron transfer reactions and revealing interfacial activity not evident in bulk solutions by conventional methods. Electrothermal mapping presents the protein thermal stability as a current–potential–temperature landscape, enabling direct comparison of the protein’s native and non-native conformational states driven by electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions. Ultimately, our work establishes a new paradigm for predicting protein behavior under heat stress at membrane-like interfaces, with far-reaching implications for biotechnology and medicine, including drug development, enzyme engineering, and protein expression, where protein stability and crevice accessibility are critical.

item.title: Nano Letters: From Resistive to FET-Type Gas Sensors: Enhanced Capability through the Addition of Terminals
item.description:
Zhen Yuan, Qihao Wang, Lijiang Zhao, Zaihua Duan, Yadong Jiang, Huiling Tai
Embodied artificial intelligence and artificial olfaction demand highly integrated gas sensors that combine sensing and computation. Conventional two-terminal chemiresistors face limitations in active modulation, miniaturization, and monolithic circuit integration, motivating the development of multiterminal field-effect transistor (FET) gas sensors. Their gate terminals enable tunable sensitivity, signal amplification, and, in suitable architectures, nonvolatile memory, offering opportunities for integrated sensing and computing. This review traces the evolution from two-terminal chemiresistors to multiterminal FET gas sensors, first comparing their structures and sensing mechanisms. It then examines how gate engineering improves sensitivity, selectivity, and integration while enabling olfactory synaptic functions, near-sensor computing, and in-sensor computing. Finally, current limitations and future research directions are discussed to guide the development of intelligent FET gas sensors for artificial olfaction.

item.title: JACS: Radical Molecular-Junction Covalent Organic Framework for Asymmetric Iodide Conversion: 100,000 Cycles in Zn-Iodine Batteries
item.description:
Liqi Bai, Ke Fan, Si-Miao Wang, Long-Zhang Dong, Hai-Ting Li, Chao Chen, Han Zhang, Yuan Xu, et al.
Aqueous Zinc–iodine batteries are promising for large-scale energy storage owing to their eco-friendliness and safety. However, conventional two-electron cathode hosts suffer from poor cycling life due to polyiodide shuttling and sluggish one-step I–/I2 redox kinetics, which limits their practical usage. Herein, we designed a molecular-junction covalent organic framework (COF) denoted as TNCOF, integrating the tetrathiafulvalene (TTF) donor and the naphthalene diimide (NDI) acceptor. Typically, TTF forms a robust radical-cationic TTF•+ structure by anchoring to iodine electrostatically. TTF•+ and electron-withdrawing NDI within the T•+NCOF molecular junction provide a driving force through an intense local electrostatic potential for the asymmetric iodine conversion (AIC) pathway (I–/I3–/I2 vs. I2/I–), markedly boosting reaction kinetics and suppressing polyiodide shuttling. The optimized T•+NCOF cathode delivers a specific capacity of 228.7 mAh g–1 at 1 A g–1 and achieves an ultralong cycling stability exceeding 100,000 cycles, which is one of the highest records in this field. In situ measurements, Peak Force Tunneling atomic force microscopy (AFM) results, and calculations confirm the robust adsorption capability of T•+NCOF and demonstrate the accelerated I3– conversion kinetics. This work establishes that a radical-cationic molecular-junction COF enables robust I3– anchoring and a unique AIC pathway, offering a novel strategy to overcome inherent stability challenges in Zinc-halogen batteries.

item.title: JACS: Composition-Driven Discovery of Multimetallic Catalysts Using Features Inspired by the Virtual Crystal Approximation
item.description:
Hou-Wei Zeng, Tian-Wei Hua, Shaofeng Li, Gui-Xiang Huang, Jie-Jie Chen, Han-Qing Yu, Jie Zeng
Structure–activity relationships built on structure-derived descriptors are a dominant paradigm in catalyst screening. However, this structure-driven framework scales poorly to multimetallic systems, where active sites are heterogeneous, dynamically reconstruct under operating conditions, and require extensive structural enumeration and system-specific descriptor engineering. Here, we introduce a composition-driven screening strategy for multimetallic catalysts using feature construction inspired by the virtual crystal approximation. Specifically, multimetallic sites are represented as composition-weighted pseudoatoms, allowing readily available elemental properties to be converted into predictive features without explicit structural modeling. Unlike elemental fractions alone, these features encode physicochemical differences among the constituent metals. We demonstrate this approach using Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) as a compositionally tunable and reconstruction-prone validation platform for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Combining the composition-derived features with symbolic regression yields an explicit expression for ranking compositions, guiding experimental identification of four high-performance PBAs. We further evaluate this strategy across six literature data sets spanning different catalyst families and reactions, independently training a model for each. Using one of the models, we screen and experimentally validate a perovskite catalyst achieving an overpotential of 189 mV at 10 mA cm–2 in acidic OER. These results demonstrate the broad applicability of virtual crystal approximation-inspired feature construction for composition-driven screening of multimetallic catalysts.

item.title: JACS: Supramolecular Regulation of the Enzymatic Dephosphorylation of Twin Phosphotyrosine Peptides
item.description:
Jordi Solà, Juan Bautista Blanco-Canosa, Nuo Cheng, Jordi Bujons, Olga Calvo, Daniel Carbajo, Ciril Jimeno, Mohan Sun, et al.
We report the design, preparation, and study of a supramolecular pseudopeptidic cage that selectively binds twin phosphotyrosine (pTyr–pTyr) peptides and modulates their enzymatic dephosphorylation in water. The receptor combines an expanded aromatic cavity specifically designed to encapsulate a twin Tyr-Tyr motif with peripheral Lys-derived ammonium groups that engage phosphate residues through electrostatic interactions. In addition to studying the cage’s binding properties through different experimental and computational techniques, we investigated the ability of the receptor to modulate the kinetics of the irreversible phosphate hydrolysis catalyzed by alkaline phosphatase (ALP). When different substrates are connected through irreversible catalytic reactions, forming a nascent network, the presence of a supramolecular protecting host, able to selectively bind these substrates, modifies the system outcome in a way that cannot be predicted from the mere comparison of individual binding constants. This leads to unexpected, emerging behaviors, altering the relative intermediate concentrations through time and therefore regulating the network response. We demonstrate the biochemical potential of this cage by protecting the twin pTyr–pTyr motif within the activation loop of JAK2 kinase from dephosphorylation by λ-protein phosphatase. Altogether, our results establish supramolecular substrate protection as an effective strategy to regulate multistep enzymatic reaction networks.

item.title: Nano Letters: Edge-Selective Growth of Monodisperse PtOX on Two-Dimensional Ni(OH)2 Nanosheets
item.description:
Jingtao Wang, Qiyun Wang, Jialu Lou, Yiming Zhang, Chao Wu, Haipeng Wang, Shibo Xi, Haofeng Xiang, et al.
Precise spatial regulation of noble-metal species is crucial for maximizing metal utilization and enabling site-specific electronic interactions. Edge sites in layered hydroxides possess distinct coordination and electronic structures, yet selectively stabilizing noble-metal species at active boundaries remains challenging. We report a photoassisted edge-selective anchoring strategy to selectively anchor highly dispersed oxidized Pt species at Ni(OH)2 nanosheet edges, forming a well-defined Ni(OH)2@PtOX edge heterointerface. Structural and spectroscopic analyses reveal edge-enriched, approximately octahedrally coordinated PtOX species stabilized by strong Pt–O–Ni coupling without perturbing the bulk lattice. In methanol oxidation, the edge-engineered catalyst exhibits higher activity, faster kinetics, and selective formate production than Ni(OH)2 and non-edge-selective Pt-loaded systems. Operando spectroscopy, electrochemical analysis, and DFT show that edge-confined PtOX promotes NiOOH formation and electronically tunes adjacent unsaturated edge-Ni sites, lowering the barrier for initial methanol activation. This work establishes two-dimensional edge engineering as a strategy for constructing functionally nonequivalent heterointerfaces.

item.title: Nano Letters: Decoding Electronic Effects of Pd through Synergistic Interstitial Alloying for Accelerated Formic Acid Oxidation
item.description:
Jun Li, Jian Dong, Jiayi Ou, Yu Zhang, Siyu Zhou, Zhengyu Xiao, Shuke Huang, Lili Han, et al.
The contradictory roles of long-range strain and short-range ligand interactions have created a complex electronic landscape that hinders the rational design of high-performance formic acid oxidation reaction catalysts. To address these issues, a synergistic interstitial alloying strategy to engineer Pd catalysts with electron-rich and electron-deficient domains was deliberately designed. Due to the unique valence electron configurations of H and P, the H, P codoped Pd catalyst exhibits mass activity of 2904 mA mg–1Pd and specific activity of 189 A m–2, outperforming commercial Pd/C by 15.7 and 13.7 times, respectively. Microkinetic analysis, density functional theory calculations, and in situ techniques demonstrate that H doping mainly induces lattice strain, while P doping dominates the ligand effect. The synergistic H, P codoping facilitates the direct dehydrogenation and suppresses CO formation. This work provides a new idea for precisely regulating the selectivity of multipathway electrochemical reactions.

item.title: Nano Letters: Double Quantum Spin Hall Phase in Bilayer ZrTe5
item.description:
Chao Chen Ye, Gábor Kalla, Marcio Costa, Jianting Ye, Jagoda Sławińska
Quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulators host helical edge states that enable dissipationless transport, but realizing multiple conducting channels in experimentally accessible materials with large band gaps remains challenging. Here, we show that AB-stacked untwisted bilayer ZrTe5 naturally realizes a double QSH phase in its energetically most stable structure, revealing an unexpected multichannel transport regime. The phase hosts two pairs of helical edge states and a doubled quantized spin Hall conductivity, with spin Chern number Cs = 2 despite the conventional Z2=0 classification. Lattice deformation tunes the system through a metallic state to a conventional QSH phase with Z2=1, enabling control of the number of helical channels. Remarkably, the quantized spin Hall response persists over an energy window substantially larger than the bulk band gap, exceeding 100 meV. Our results establish bilayer ZrTe5 as an experimentally accessible multichannel QSH system in which interlayer coupling and lattice deformation control topological edge transport.

item.title: Nano Letters: Liquid-Phase Connectivity in Porous Membranes Enables High-Rate Acidic Zero-Gap CO2 Electrolysis
item.description:
Hao Yu, Ziwen Mei, Kang Liu, Qin Chen, Min Liu
High-current-density acidic CO2 electrolysis in zero-gap membrane–electrode assemblies is strongly limited by coupled water and ion transport across the membrane. Here, we use a hydrophilic porous mixed cellulose ester membrane to replace conventional dense Nafion, establishing continuous liquid-filled pathways across the membrane thickness. Multiphysics simulations show that this network sustains proton supply and suppresses cathode-side K+ accumulation as current density increases. Dynamic wetting, H3O+ and K+ diffusion, impedance, and in situ infrared measurements consistently verify rapid liquid-mediated transport and a more highly hydrated membrane environment. The resulting electrolyzer maintains a CO Faradaic efficiency of 93.6% at 800 mA cm–2, operates for approximately 50 h at 500 mA cm–2, and remains stable for more than 100 h at 100 mA cm–2. This work presents a membrane-level strategy for engineering continuous liquid-phase pathways, offering a route to regulate coupled water and ion transport in high-current-density acidic CO2 electrolysis.

item.title: Nano Letters: Room-Temperature Highly Anisotropic In-Plane Electron Transport in a π-Stacked Metal–Organic Nanosheet
item.description:
Qiuping Xie, Gonghua Hong, Yun Yin, Yiran Pu, Yajing Zhang, Xiaoling Wang, Yunxiang He, Ian Manners, et al.
Directional control of electron transport in solids is a long-standing goal in condensed-matter physics and electronic engineering. In two-dimensional systems, strongly directional chiral edge transport has so far been achieved only in quantum Hall states, which require strong magnetic fields or extremely low temperatures. We report an ultrathin metal–organic nanosheet (MPhix, ∼3.4 nm) exhibiting strong in-plane conduction anisotropy at room temperature and zero magnetic field. MPhix self-assembles from bismuth ions and bio-derived ellagic acid into a crystalline sheet, where π–π stacking of organic linkers creates unique one-dimensional electron pathways. Conductive atomic force microscopy visualizes channel-aligned high-current stripes and quantifies a 21–34× in-plane anisotropy at 298 K and 0 T. Leveraging bio-derived molecular stacking for strongly anisotropic in-plane electron transport without magnets or cryogenics, this work outlines a sustainable strategy for next-generation quantum materials.

item.title: ACS Nano: Ferrohydrodynamic Microfluidics for Multiscale Bioparticle Separation and Phenotyping
item.description:
Yuhao Zhang, Yong Teng, Kenan Song, Xianqiao Wang, Xianyan Chen, Yuhua Liu, Yiping Zhao, He Li, et al.
Ferrohydrodynamic microfluidics uses magnetic nanoparticles dispersed in ferrofluids to generate magnetic buoyancy forces for continuous manipulation of diamagnetic particles and magnetically labeled cells. These forces enable separation and phenotyping of cells, extracellular vesicles, and other bioparticles across length scales, although downstream molecular and functional compatibility depends on controlling ferrofluid exposure and residual nanoparticles. This Perspective examines the evolution of ferrofluid-based microfluidics from size-based enrichment toward quantitative physical and molecular phenotyping. We assess key technical and translational challenges, including biocompatibility, scalable and reproducible device architectures, nanoparticle depletion, quality control, and clinical translation. We also define application-specific priorities and discuss how engineered ferrofluids, additive manufacturing, machine learning, and molecular readouts could broaden the versatility of these platforms for precision bioanalysis.

item.title: ACS Nano: Molecularly Programmed Piezoelectric Peptide Interfaces Couple Energy Conversion with Cell Recognition for Neural Regeneration
item.description:
Rongrong Wu, Xiaojun Cai, Kexiao Yu, Wenhui Liu, Judith Zubia-Aranburu, Feiyi Zhang, Kjeld Kaj Klompmaker, Lasse Hyldgaard Klausen, et al.
Electrical regulation of tissue regeneration occurs at dynamic biointerfaces, where cells integrate mechanical, biochemical, and electrical cues from their surrounding microenvironment. Engineering biodegradable materials that simultaneously establish bioactive interfaces and convert externally applied mechanical energy into localized bioelectrical signals remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we establish a molecular programming strategy for constructing bioactive piezoelectric biointerfaces through sequence-defined peptide self-assembly. Guided by multiscale molecular simulations, an amphiphilic peptide hierarchically assembles into noncentrosymmetric two-dimensional nanopatches in which electromechanical energy conversion, cell recognition, and intrinsic antioxidant activity emerge cooperatively from a single supramolecular architecture. Upon clinically compatible ultrasound stimulation, the engineered biointerfaces generate physiologically relevant electrical potentials while maintaining radical-scavenging activity without inducing reactive oxygen species. The localized bioelectrical communication due to their desired cell-adhesiveness activates calcium signaling, cytoskeletal reorganization, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immunomodulatory programs, leading to enhanced cell migration in vitro and coordinated axonal regeneration, remyelination, angiogenesis, and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in rats. Generally, a general molecular design principle is established linking peptide sequence, hierarchical assembly, and biointerface function, demonstrating that electromechanical conversion and biological communication can be coprogrammed within biodegradable supramolecular materials for neural regeneration.

item.title: JACS: In Situ STEM Imaging of Colloidal Crystals Based on Programmable Atom Equivalents
item.description:
Arindam Raj, Ana Clara Zampirolli Leal, Nathan D. Rosenmann, Christopher Sharpe, Roberto dos Reis, Tirzah Abbott, George Winstone, Vinayak P. Dravid, et al.
It is challenging to image the assembly of colloidal crystals composed of programmable atom equivalents (PAEs) using electron microscopy (EM). PAEs typically consist of nanoparticle cores densely functionalized with radially oriented DNA shells, which assemble in the liquid phase via DNA bonds. EM requires high-vacuum conditions, and electron beams can damage soft materials like nucleic acids. Here, we present a liquid-phase scanning transmission electron microscopy (LPSTEM) method for imaging PAEs composed of ∼5 nm gold nanoparticle cores in solution, enabling the direct investigation of their DNA-directed assembly processes. This system is particularly well-suited for in situ studies of soft-matter dynamics because the gold nanoparticle cores provide strong electron contrast. Using a nanofluidic liquid cell, the nucleation and growth of PAE assemblies, governed via the principles of colloidal crystal engineering with DNA, were directly observed. Imaging conditions were established to resolve colloidal assemblies in liquid while also characterizing electron-beam-induced damage under both conventional STEM and STEM-in-SEM conditions. Quantitative image analysis reveals changes in local coordination during crystal growth and subsequent beam-induced dissociation. Complementary ex situ simulations corroborate that radiolytic species generated in the buffer are major contributors to beam-induced damage. Together, these results establish a versatile and accessible platform for probing the in situ dynamics of PAE assembly in liquids, with broad applicability to the study of other soft nanomaterials and composites relevant to sensing, actuation, energy storage, catalysis, and medicine.

item.title: JACS: Accessing Alkyl Linkers for Macrocyclic Peptide Synthesis via Nickel-Mediated Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization
item.description:
Yun Hong, Zhenning Li, Shane Plunkett, Danielle M. Schultz, Dipannita Kalyani, Amelie Dion, Mary P. Watson
The rise of macrocyclic peptides as a therapeutic modality has exposed gaps in the synthetic chemistry toolbox available for drug discovery teams to rapidly explore diverse linkers for structural optimization. In contrast to the thioether linkers common in peptide leads identified from mRNA display, all-carbon linkers are desirable for imparting solubility and stability, but existing approaches suffer from limited amino acid diversity, incompatibility with solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), stereochemical loss, multistep requirements, or restricted linker placement. We report a Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization (D2AM) to install alkyl linkers via C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation. This method uses pyridinium monomers derived from commercial amino acids that are stable to SPPS for the seamless synthesis of complex macrocyclic and polycyclic peptides with conservation of stereochemistry. This deaminative method is anticipated to accelerate optimization of peptide macrocycle structure in drug discovery.

item.title: ACS Nano: Immune and Stromal Barriers to Active Nanoparticle Targeting of Claudin-4 in Tumors
item.description:
David Angarita, Hanmant Gaikwad, David Siegel, Hanna Mattanovich, Aislinn Warmka, Joshua B. Judson, Kyle A. Sullivan, Elizabeth R. Woodruff, et al.
Nanoparticles with targeting ligands can act as “magic bullets” to selectively target tumor cells, a concept that has captivated the drug delivery field for decades. Using cell culture, engineered mouse models, and spatial imaging, we studied how cellular interactions influence targeting of claudin-4 (CLDN4), a key ovarian cancer target. We coupled the C-terminal domain of Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (cCPE), a high-affinity CLDN4 binder, to ∼60 nm dextran iron oxide nanoworms (CLIO NW) via click chemistry. Targeted NWs had nanomolar affinity for CLDN4 and specifically targeted CLDN4+ cells in culture and 3D spheroids. After systemic injection in mice, targeted NWs exhibited a long plasma half-life. In bilateral CLDN4+/CLDN4– xenograft tumors, targeted NWs accumulated more in CLDN4+ tumors but were also taken up by Kupffer cells in the liver and CD45+ immune cells in both tumors. Repeating the study with anti-CLDN4 IgG-decorated NWs, we again observed high in vitro specificity but low in vivo selectivity, as confirmed by optical and magnetic resonance imaging. Spatial proteomic analysis of tumors showed that NWs mainly accumulate in tumor cells, immune cells, and myofibroblasts, with tumor core cells mostly negative for NWs. Cell stress and metabolic profiles remain unchanged after the uptake. Coculture of CLDN4+ tumor cells and macrophages replicated the limited selectivity of targeted NWs in vivo and suggested that complement opsonization contributes to limited selectivity. Overall, stromal and immune uptake hinder CLDN4 targeting. Future efforts should focus on understanding and inhibiting nanoparticle uptake pathways to develop molecularly targeted nanomedicine.

item.title: ACS Nano: Collective Plasmon Resonances in Hierarchically Doped Metal-Oxide Nanocrystal Metasurfaces
item.description:
Yujin Park, Tanner A. Wilcoxson, Yina Wu, Jordan A. Hachtel, Tanay Paul, Hans A. Bechtel, Stephanie N. Gilbert Corder, M. Wren Berry, et al.
Plasmonic nanocrystal (NC) assemblies produce collective plasmon resonances (CPRs), amplifying light–matter interactions beyond the single-NC limit. Structural and compositional disorder in self-assembled NCs effectively diversify optical responses via inhomogeneous near fields, a heterogeneity that provides a degree of versatility that can benefit applications in sensing and photochemistry. How near-field coupling between spectrally detuned plasmonic NCs sculpts emergent CPR modes and far-field responses remains unexplored. Here, we leverage optical and electron spectroscopies to investigate near-field coupling in hierarchically doped assemblies of plasmonic metal oxide NCs. Similarly doped NCs form coherently resonating subsets underlying CPR hybridization, and near-field coupling between dissimilarly doped NCs locally enhances near fields in a way that cannot be explained by the NC mixing ratio alone. Optical simulations predict that individual NCs are polarized not at their native localized surface plasmon resonance frequency but instead at each hybrid-mode frequency, with coupling either enhancing or suppressing extinction depending on the neighboring NC environment. We experimentally observe this local optical heterogeneity using synchrotron infrared nanospectroscopy, and visualize the coupling-modified near fields by spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy. We further develop a coupled oscillator model that analytically describes CPR hybridization and quantifies how the degree of CPR hybridization redistributes the dipole response of each NC species, an approach that could be generalized to other compositions, such as mixed metallic nanoparticle assemblies. These findings reveal how near-field coupling in heterogeneous NC assemblies governs the emergence of the ensemble response from local to macroscopic scales, providing a conceptual framework for tailored plasmonic metamaterials.

item.title: ACS Nano: Surface Termination Controls Symmetric Block Copolymer Transport through Nanopores
item.description:
Sang Yup Lee, Uiseok Hwang, Tae-Young Heo, Théophile Ienn, Julien Bernard, Robert A. Riggleman, Daeyeon Lee
Understanding how polymer architecture governs transport through nanopores is essential for nanocomposite fabrication, membrane design, and functional coatings. However, the effect of the nanoscale structure of copolymers on chain transport through nanoporous media remains poorly understood. In this study, we demonstrate that simply inverting the surface orientation of lamellar poly(styrene-block-2-vinylpyridine) (PS-b-P2VP) diblock copolymers, composed of two monomers with strongly contrasting affinities for SiO2, at the entrance of a nanoporous packing of SiO2 nanoparticles significantly alters the kinetics of capillary rise infiltration (CaRI). Using in situ spectroscopic ellipsometry, we find that infiltration of the PS-b-P2VP symmetric diblock copolymer into SiO2 nanoparticle (NP) packings is significantly faster when the P2VP domain is the top layer of the block copolymer film and is therefore the first to contact the NPs, compared to when the PS domain is the top layer. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations reveal that this difference originates from block-specific adsorption pathways that reorganize the nanophase structure around NPs: P2VP-first infiltration forms thin adsorbed layers that drive PS into the pore interiors, producing larger PS-rich regions with greater apparent connectivity, which is associated with a higher upward chain flux. In contrast, PS-first infiltration produces thicker P2VP layers that result in smaller, more fragmented PS-rich regions and a lower upward chain flux. Above the order–disorder transition (ODT), or upon silanizing NPs to neutralize surface affinity, the rate difference disappears. These findings demonstrate how the interplay between nanoscale domain configuration and polymer–surface affinity governs infiltration dynamics, providing mechanistic insight into controlling transport in nanostructured block copolymers and into designing high-loading composites, selective membranes, and functional coatings with controlled transport pathways.

item.title: JACS: News Spotlights, powered by C&EN
item.description: JACS

item.title: JACS: Defect-Mediated On–Off Growth in Tautomeric Crystallization: The Curious Case of Theophylline Monohydrate
item.description:
Si Li, Arshia Nosrati, Qizan Chen, Sungil Hong, Giannis Mpourmpakis, Jeetain Mittal, Jeffrey D. Rimer
Crystal growth is inherently sensitive to interfacial structure, yet it remains poorly understood how intrinsic molecular heterogeneity in tautomeric materials translates into dynamic growth behaviors. Here, we combine microfluidics, in situ atomic force microscopy (AFM), molecular dynamics (MD), and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the crystallization of theophylline monohydrate, which exhibits a minor tautomer (TP-N9, percent-level) coexisting in growth solutions with the dominant lattice-forming species (TP-N7). Facet-resolved measurements show that the (101̅) and (103̅) surfaces exhibit markedly different growth kinetics owing to their distinct interfacial structures, including transitions between arrested and active growth states. On basal (011) and (01̅1) planes, we observe anisotropic step propagation arising from direction-dependent molecular packing at step edges, which impose conformational constraints on solute incorporation into surface growth sites. Despite its low abundance, the TP-N9 tautomer functions as a growth inhibitor and exerts a disproportionate, facet-dependent influence on surface growth. MD simulations indicate that solute adsorption strength alone cannot explain growth rate anisotropy; instead, adsorption in growth-incompatible configurations appears critical, with growth rates governed by the energetic barriers for post-adsorption rearrangement into registry with the crystal lattice. Time-resolved measurements across a range of synthesis conditions revealed defects that transiently pin advancing steps, persist through partial overgrowth, and create local strain, which we attribute to TP-N9 adsorption. These collective effects give rise to spatially heterogeneous growth and dissolution and, macroscopically, drive defect-mediated on–off growth through dynamic shifts in faceting. These results reveal how trace-level tautomeric heterogeneity can redirect crystal growth through facet-dependent incorporation and defect-mediated kinetic regulation.

item.title: ACS Nano: Efficient Membrane Separation of Rare Earth Ions in Engineered Macrocycle Channels
item.description:
Jiachen Feng, Julia Chung, Zhongwu Li, Martin Conda-Sheridan, Yuhao Li, Aleksandr Noy
Rare earth elements (REEs) are critical components in advanced technologies and are notoriously difficult to separate due to their similar chemical properties. This study explored the design and application of a series of synthetic macrocycles to achieve selective lanthanide separation in a macroscopic biomimetic membrane. We synthesized a set of macrocycles that can integrate into lipid bilayers and demonstrate distinct variations in ion permeability attributed to differences in structural flexibility and specific functional groups. Notably, one of the macrocycles exhibits an 18-fold difference in permeability between neodymium and dysprosium ions, underscoring its potential for selective REE separation. This selectivity was further translated into macroscopic separations in a scalable droplet emulsion-based membrane that achieved a 22-fold enrichment of dysprosium over neodymium from a multicomponent lanthanide mixture under an applied electric field. This work advances the understanding of macrocyclic ligand design, highlighting the balance between molecular rigidity, conformational freedom, and chemical functionalization as key factors in enhancing the selective transport of REEs.

item.title: ACS Nano: Single-Crystal-Like Giant-Grain Oxide Semiconductors
item.description:
Kyungmoon Kwak, I. Sak Lee, Si Hyun Park, Jae-Eun Pi, Sooji Nam, Yongduck Kim, Ji Hun Choi, Ju Hyun Lee, et al.
Controlling grain size in crystalline oxide semiconductors (COSs) has long been a fundamental challenge, with lateral grain dimensions typically limited to several hundred nanometers. Here, we report nucleation-suppression-driven grain engineering in quaternary Al-incorporated In–Ga–O (AIGO) to obtain giant-grain oxide semiconductors (GOS). GOS exhibits giant grains of approximately 18 μm with locally single-crystal-like domains, substantially exceeding the TFT channel dimensions (5 × 5 μm) while being realized through a back-end-of-line (BEOL)-compatible process below 400 °C. Back-channel-etched (BCE) TFTs based on GOS exhibit enhanced electrical performance, with the field-effect mobility increasing from 32.06 cm2 V–1 s–1 in conventional crystalline IGO TFTs to 41.08 cm2 V–1 s–1. More importantly, giant-grain engineering markedly improves device reliability, reducing the threshold-voltage shift (ΔVTH) from 7.21 to 1.38 V under positive bias temperature stress (PBTS), from 8.79 to 0.95 V under negative bias illumination stress (NBIS), and from 10.21 to 1.51 V under negative bias temperature illumination stress (NBTIS). In contrast, excessive Al incorporation suppresses crystallization, resulting in an amorphous phase and degraded device characteristics, highlighting the critical role of composition in balancing crystallization and carrier transport. These findings demonstrate the potential of giant-grain engineering for highly reliable, BEOL-compatible oxide electronics.

item.title: JACS: Terahertz Stimulation Enhances Nanopore Capture Rate via Mitigating Voltage-Induced Water Compression
item.description:
Changxiong Huang, Huan Chen, Jun Luo, Yewen Juan, Jun Fan, Xiao Cheng Zeng
Nanopore sensing has emerged as a powerful tool for proteomic analysis, yet controlling molecular translocation, particularly for neutral residues, remains a significant challenge. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the translocation of electrically neutral peptides and amino acids, and to elucidate how nanoslit geometry and applied voltage jointly regulate the process from both kinetic and thermodynamic perspectives. As the applied voltage increases from 0 to 1 V, the biomolecule capture time doubles, whereas the dwell time is reduced by half. Potential-of-mean-force calculations reveal a higher entry barrier and a lower exit barrier. Further analyses of solvent density and the corresponding bulk-equivalent pressure show that increasing the voltage or narrowing the nanoslit raises the density of the confined solution, generating a bulk-equivalent static-pressure differential that increases resistance to molecular entry while reducing resistance to exit. To relieve this voltage-induced compression, we apply an external terahertz (THz) electromagnetic stimulation, which effectively shortens the capture time by lowering the entry barrier from 48.49 to 38.76 kJ/mol. This study provides molecular-level insights into nanopore translocation and offers practical strategies to enhance molecular capture, potentially advancing nanopore proteomics and informing related applications.
